messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 71
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Insurance Agent
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Stranger Interaction: Talking to strangers, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Prevention: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Robert is a 71-year-old insurance agent who lives alone and has spent most of his adult life priding himself on being steady, polite, and hard to rattle. In the first sessions, though, it became clear that the fears bringing him to treatment reach back to childhood, when the person responsible for his care was also the person who physically abused him. He described a house organized around unpredictability. He would hear an adult coming in unsteadily, catch the smell of alcohol before he saw him, and know from the set of a voice or the scrape of movement that he might be grabbed, hit, or cornered. What remains most painful to Robert is not only the violence itself but the fact that it came from someone he had depended on. He had come to believe that he was betrayed by someone he trusted, and he still speaks with bitterness about how the adults around him never stopped it and how the person responsible faced no real consequences.

In the years since, the memory has never settled into the past. Robert does not recall it as a single story so much as in abrupt pieces that arrive without warning: a hand at his sleeve, the sound of someone entering, the thick smell of alcohol. At times, when the memory catches him, it feels more vivid than whatever is in front of him, almost more real than ordinary life. He can sometimes smell again what he smelled then, and those sensory fragments land with such force that talking to strangers, hearing sirens outside, or catching alcohol on someone’s breath can feel charged before he has even told himself why. Those moments do not just remind him of what happened; they confirm his sense that the original betrayal is still alive inside him and that the people who did this escaped accountability.

Because the memories come in these sensory bursts, Robert has spent years trying not to leave his mind unoccupied. He keeps the radio on, fills quiet moments with paperwork, and structures his evenings so that there is always something to focus on. He also avoids television programs, films, or articles that involve child abuse, domestic violence, or even scenes of drunken confrontation because he knows how easily a fragment can break loose and take over the room. When the smells and flashes still get through, he finds himself silently repeating little mental rituals, a private sequence of words and counting that he believes might keep bad things from happening again. Yet having to do this leaves him feeling ashamed and defeated; to Robert it is proof that his own body has become an enemy, reacting as though danger is present even when he is sitting safely in his apartment.

That conviction feeds the way he moves through the world now. He is certain that if his body can surge into alarm so suddenly, then threat must be close by even when other people seem unconcerned. He listens closely at home for any sound that might mean someone is entering. If footsteps pause outside his door, he stiffens immediately. In ordinary situations with unfamiliar people, especially if a stranger approaches him too quickly, he feels threatened before a word is exchanged. At the office, where part of his work as an insurance agent still involves meeting new clients, he finds himself studying the doorway, the tone of a man’s voice, whether there is any trace of alcohol on someone’s clothes. Sirens outside the building can jolt him into a full-body reaction as if something terrible is about to happen, and once he is in that state he becomes even more convinced that strangers are dangerous and that his system is detecting something others miss.

This constant scanning seems to call the past up more readily. The more Robert listens for intruders and watches people for signs of menace, the more sudden fragments of the abuse break through, vivid and sensory, and the more potent his triggers become. A stranger asking an ordinary question in the lobby, a siren while he is driving to a client visit, or the smell of alcohol in an elevator can pull him at once toward the old conclusion that trust is unsafe and that harm comes from people who should know better. In response he doubles down on the habits that have narrowed his life: staying mentally busy, avoiding media, repeating his rituals. Those strategies bring short-lived relief, but they also keep him watching, listening, and bracing, which leaves him feeling under siege by both his surroundings and his own body.

What finally brought Robert to seek help was a recent episode at work when a prospective client stepped toward his desk unexpectedly, carrying the stale smell of liquor on his coat, just as sirens passed outside. Robert froze, lost the thread of the meeting, and spent the rest of the day shaken and preoccupied by fragmented images he could not control. He worries now that his world is shrinking around him, that he is becoming a fearful old man who cannot trust anyone and cannot trust his own reactions. At the same time, he says quietly that he wants “one room in my life where the past isn’t already waiting for me,” and that hope is what has kept him coming back.
